\section{Proportionality, the Core, and Stability}\label{sec:prop}
\aibanner

The notions above are imposed by a designer who fixes demographic constraints in advance. A complementary, \emph{game-theoretic} family lets \emph{coalitions of individuals} certify their own fair treatment, removing the need to pre-specify protected groups.

\subsection{Proportional fairness and the core}

Chen et al.~\citep{chen2019proportionally} introduced \emph{proportional fairness} for centroid clustering, borrowing the notion of the \emph{core} from cooperative game theory: any sufficiently large group of points is entitled to its own center. Given $k$ centers, a subset $S\subseteq P$ with $|S|\ge \lceil n/k\rceil$ is a \emph{blocking coalition} if some $y\in P$ satisfies $d(x,y)&lt;d(x,C)$ for every $x\in S$ --- all of $S$ would strictly prefer $y$. A solution is \emph{proportionally fair} (in the core) if it admits no blocking coalition.

Exact proportional solutions need not exist, motivating $\rho$-approximate proportionality, where a coalition blocks only if every member improves by more than a factor $\rho$. Chen et al.~\citep{chen2019proportionally} showed a simple \emph{greedy capture} procedure attains a $(1+\sqrt{2})$-approximate core and proved separations from classical optimality. ~\citep{DBLP:conf/icalp/Micha020} revisited the model, tightening bounds for Euclidean instances and clarifying the price of proportionality relative to the optimal $k$-median cost.

Because proportional fairness needs no protected attributes, it is attractive when group labels are unavailable or contested; the trade-off is that it constrains \emph{coalitions} rather than demographic balance, and the two need not coincide.

\subsection{Preference- and stability-based fairness}

A related line treats each individual's \emph{preference} over clusters as the primitive. Ahmadi et al.~\citep{ahmadi2022individual} formalized \emph{individual-preference (IP) stability}: a clustering is IP-stable if no point's average distance to its own cluster exceeds its average distance to any other cluster, so no individual would, on average, prefer to defect. They characterize when IP-stable clusterings exist and give approximation algorithms --- exact on the line and bounded-factor in general metrics --- alongside hardness results. Conceptually these definitions import \emph{envy-freeness} and stable matching into clustering, linking fair clustering to stability in coalition formation.
